title: Noisy Interactive Graph Search

problem.claim: Locate an initially unknown target node in a graph through sequential human reachability queries while minimizing query complexity and ensuring accuracy.

gap.claim: Existing interactive graph search must account for human workers making mistakes when answering reachability queries.

contributions.claim: A query-node selection method that pushes the search process as much as possible.
An online method for inferring the target node after each newly collected answer.
A theoretical analysis establishing a near-optimal query-complexity guarantee up to a constant factor.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their approach has near-optimal query complexity up to a constant factor.
The authors report superior performance in extensive experiments on two real datasets.

narrative_sequence.summary: Interactive graph search locates an initially unknown target node using human intelligence and sequential reachability queries.
Human workers may answer reachability queries incorrectly, motivating a noisy formulation.
The noisy search problem seeks low query complexity while maintaining accuracy.
The paper proposes query-node selection and online target-inference methods.
The authors report a near-optimal theoretical bound and superior results on two real datasets.

source_observation.claim: Human-in-the-loop graph search can be modeled as a noisy sequential-query problem.

interpretation.claim: Search procedures should incorporate answer errors rather than assume every human response is correct.

application.claim: Human-guided graph-search systems may benefit from jointly designing query selection and online inference under noisy responses.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the error model, applicable graph assumptions, or conditions under which the methods achieve their guarantees.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the human-error model.
The abstract does not state the graph assumptions or exact query-complexity bound.
The abstract does not identify the two real datasets or experimental metrics.
